author: Frances Mao
title: Northern Ireland live: controversial Orange Order march in Portadown delayed amid huge counter-protest - NewsBreak
text:
By Frances Mao ,
2 hours ago People block the Garvaghy road, a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant town of Portadown, ahead of the Orange Order march Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters 10.34am BST
Orange Order march delayed as protesters block route With counter-protesters still blocking Garvaghy Road, there’s uncertainty over whether the Orangemen will carry out their march.
The court had ruled for the procession to kick off at 8am and to finish by 9.30am but it does not appear that the group of 35 Orangemen marchers have even set off from their starting point at Drumcree Church.
My colleague Lisa O’Caroll reports that Northern Ireland Cool FM is saying the Orange Order is in talks with police after they were told that the route down Garvaghy Road, which is blockaded by protestors, may not be possible after all.
Orangemen had formed up at Drumcree Church but have now gone back inside as talks continue.
The Garvaghy Road remains blocked, and it’s understood there will be no movement any time soon, with the Orange Order still planning to march.
The BBC is reporting that a member of the group said they would wait on the advice of police to tell them when they could start the march.
Updated at 10.45am BST
10.27am BST
Democratic Unionist Party blasts counter-protest organised to block march DUP Leader Rt. Hon. Gavin Robinson MP has condemned first minister Michelle O’Neill over remarks which he believes are obstructing a legal parade down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
“A first minister’s duty is to uphold lawful decisions, not inflame opposition to them,” Robinson.
“The legal position is now unequivocal. 35 Orangemen can walk in silence along Garvaghy Road. The Court of Appeal found that the injunction had been granted in error, and the High Court subsequently confirmed that the Parades Commission determination must be respected.
Yet Michelle O’Neill described that outcome as “disgraceful”, claimed an Orange procession was being ‘forced’ through the area and declared: “There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever.”
Those words were followed by organised obstruction of the road, while Breandán Mac Cionnaith instructed people to sit down, link arms and return if removed by police.
Michelle O’Neill then addressed the gathering, urged it to “stay strong” and repeated the “no going back” chant.
10.23am BST
Northern Ireland secretary heading to Belfast Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant is on his way to Belfast, leaving the Labour party conference in Liverpool to address the tensions.
Speaking to the BBC in Liverpool, he said he is taking the situation “very, very seriously”.
Calling for calm he said it was “important that everybody abides by the law”.
“I would urge people to cooperate with the police. I would say that on both sides incidentally.”
9.51am BST
PM Andy Burnham appeals for 'calm on all sides' The prime minister has just been speaking on the BBC about the parade, calling for calm to prevail.
“I know it’s a tense situation. We do appeal for calm on all sides,” he told Laura Kuenssberg on her politics show.
“There have been big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards.
“So, obviously, a challenging situation today, but it’s very important that we work to bring calm.”
He also noted the authority of the decision made by the Parades Commission, which he said had been upheld by the courts.
I’ll have a post laying out the legal reasoning of the judges next.
9.43am BST
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill, at the scene of the counter-protest this morning also spoke alongside Mary Lou McDonald.
O’Neill said she had called on Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant to intervene.
She told reporters: “Does anybody think that this is a good idea? No right-minded person would make this decision.
“I still do not know the answer to this question - why, after 28 years of determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back onto this community?”
Updated at 9.43am BST
9.27am BST
Local MP Carla Lockhart, from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, posted this morning on X describing the marchers as a “dignified grouping of men, walking silently down Garvaghy Road”.
She included a photo of the small group in suits, wearing orange silk sashes and black bowler hats and carrying a banner.
“There is no threat, no triumphalism, not even music. There is nothing to fear. The rule of law must prevail,” she wrote.
Updated at 9.43am BST
9.22am BST
While the Orangemen march has begun, there’s no sign yet of the two groups coming within sight of each other.
The Parades Commission had ruled that the march could go from 8am to 9.30am.
Police officers and vans are present at the counter-protest along Garvaghy Road, where at least hundreds have gathered to block the route. There’s a police helicopter hovering overhead.
Earlier, police had blasted out a message over speakers that taking part in the counter- demonstration could be a criminal offence, a warning that hasn’t dispelled those gathered.
Updated at 10.08am BST
9.03am BST
Just 35 Orangemen protesters authorised for march The Parades Commission has authorised a small group – of just 35 Orangemen – to march along the road silently this morning. They’ve not been allowed bands or supporters.
The Parades Commission is the independent body in Northern Ireland adjudicating on controversial marches and protest – because of a history of such events being a trigger for wider sectarian violence.
Northern Ireland saw three decades of conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists.
Garvaghy Road had been a major flashpoint of the unrest in the late 1990s.
But the Commission this year determined that the Orange Order could make the return leg of their route through this part of town, having barred the Order the last almost 30 years.
Updated at 9.28am BST
9.01am BST
My colleague Lisa O’Carroll has been reporting from Garvaghy Road this morning, where senior Sinn Féin leaders had joined the counter-protest.
Leader of Sinn Féin, Mary Lou McDonald, said the appeal court’s decision to allow the march go ahead was “disgraceful”.
“The decision tonight to overturn the court ruling, and force an unwanted orange march through the Garvaghy Road is disgraceful.
“This march is steeped in a history of hate, sectarian violence, and murder, and championed by Unionist leaders”.
8.48am BST
A history of disorder with the parade The Orange Order, one of the most prominent organisations within unionism, insisted that the Garvaghy Road is part of its traditional marching route but the event is opposed by many Catholic residents who live there.
The parade was last permitted down Garvaghy Road in 1998 after a wave of violence followed clashes on the street, with thousands of public order incidents across Northern Ireland including murders.
A ruling by the Parades Commission permitting the Orange Order to march on Garvaghy Road was upheld at around 2.15am after an appeals court overturned a ruling by the High Court on Saturday to allow the procession, despite fears it could spark fresh sectarian violence.
8.44am BST
Loyalist march takes place for first time since 1998 The controversial loyalist march down a mainly Catholic Road in Northern Ireland, banned for almost 30 years because of violence, has begun after an appeals court ruled in the small hours of Sunday morning it was legal.
Protestors braved heavy rain in Portadown on Sunday morning as they gathered at the scene of the contentious Drumcree parade, which starts at Drumcree church and proceeds through the town including the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
The crowds, many of them wearing balaclavas, clustered in large groups along Garvaghy Road in the hours leading up to the start of the parade at 8am.
First minister Michelle O’Neill said the original decision to allow the march was “primitive stuff in the year 2026” while unionists said Catholics had “nothing to fear”.
8.35am BST
Hundreds of protesters had gatherered overnight on Garvaghy Road to block passage to the group of Protestant marchers.
Pictures from the scene show a sizeable crowd with protesters linking arms several rows deep.
Sinn Féin has posted some footage from the protest, describing it as “thousands standing proudly in solidarity with Garvaghy Road residents.
“Peace and progress must be protected. We reject unwanted orange marches.”
Updated at 8.41am BST
8.24am BST
Northern Ireland’s First Minister Michelle O’Neill had condemned the late- night court ruling allowing the march to proceed.
“Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever.”
Sinn Féin supported the residents of Garvaghy Road to protest against “this unwanted sectarian march,” she said.
Updated at 8.41am BST
8.17am BST
Opening summary Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the latest news in Northern Ireland after a Protestant march was permitted to go ahead on Sunday for the first time in almost 30 years.
The original dispute over the route of the Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown became one of the defining flashpoints of the conflict in Northern Ireland.
Here is a quick recap of the latest:
A ​Protestant parade may proceed through a Catholic area, Northern Ireland’s high court ruled early on Sunday , reversing a temporary ban on the highly charged march in ⁠an area that has historically been a flashpoint of sectarian disputes.
The high court dismissed a new application to stop the Orange Order from going through the area of ⁠Portadown after the court of appeal vacated a temporary injunction granted on Saturday to residents who opposed the parade.
Residents ​of the Garvaghy Road area had challenged ‌Friday’s ruling by Northern Ireland’s Parades ‌Commission that permitted the Orange Order to march along their road , a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant ‌town, overturning an almost 30-year ban on the route.
A crowd gathered on the Garvaghy Road early on Sunday morning to protest against the ruling to allow the march. In the crowd were Northern Ireland first minister Michelle O’Neill, who is also vice-president of the Irish nationalist Sinn Féin party.
The party’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, posted a video on social media of the gathering . “Although the forces of darkness may want ‌to stop us creating a new united Ireland, they will fail,” McDonald told a crowd of protesters in the clip, posted on X.
Annual attempts by the ⁠Protestant Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region before ​the route was banned in ​1998, the year the Good Friday agreement ​largely ended the three decades of violence known as the “Troubles”.
The Parades Commission’s determination on ​Friday stipulated that a smaller-than-usual ‌35 people could ​take part in the march, ​that it should begin by 8am (0700 GMT) and finish by 9:30am, and that no supporters or bands would be allowed.
summary: My colleague Lisa O’Caroll reports that Northern Ireland Cool FM is saying the Orange Order is in talks with police after they were told that the route down Garvaghy Road, which is blockaded by protestors, may not be possible after all. The Parades Commission is the independent body in Northern Ireland adjudicating on controversial marches and protest – because of a history of such events being a trigger for wider sectarian violence.
